paragraphs: Parental affection is perhaps the blindest form of perverse self-love; for, unlike the French, we do not have two terms (L’amour propre, L’amour de soi meme) to distinguish the pursuit of a natural and reasonable desire from the ignorant calculations of weakness. Parents often love their children in the most brutish way, and sacrifice every duty they owe to others in order to push them forward in the world — to promote, such is the perversity of unprincipled prejudices, the future welfare of the very beings whose present existence they embitter by the most despotic exercise of power. Power, indeed, is always true to its vital principle, for in every shape it wants to reign without check or question. Its throne is built over a dark abyss that no eye may dare to explore, lest the baseless structure should totter under investigation. Obedience, unconditional obedience, is the watchword of tyrants of every kind, and to make “assurance doubly sure,” one kind of despotism props up another. Tyrants would have cause to tremble if reason became the rule of duty in any of the relations of life, for the light might spread until full day appeared. And when it did, how men would smile at the sight of the bugbears that startled them during the night of ignorance or the twilight of timid inquiry!

Indeed, in many minds parental affection is only a pretext for tyrannizing where it can be done with impunity; for only good and wise men are content with the kind of respect that will bear discussion. Convinced that they have a right to what they insist on, they do not fear reason or dread the close examination of questions that come back to natural justice, because they firmly believe that the more enlightened the human mind becomes, the deeper just and simple principles will take root. They do not settle for expedients, or grant that what is true in theory can be false in practice; but, scorning the shifts of the moment, they calmly wait until time, sanctioning innovation, silences the hiss of selfishness or envy.

If the power to reflect on the past and to dart the keen eye of contemplation into the future is the great privilege of man, it must be granted that some people enjoy this prerogative only to a very limited degree. Everything now looks wrong to them; and, unable to tell the possible from the monstrous, they fear where fear has no place, running from the light of reason as if it were a firebrand; yet the limits of the possible have never been defined so as to stop the hand of the bold innovator.

Woman, however, a slave to prejudice in every situation, seldom shows enlightened maternal affection; for she either neglects her children or spoils them with improper indulgence. Besides, the affection some women have for their children is, as I have called it before, often very brutish, for it roots out every spark of humanity. Justice, truth, everything is sacrificed by these Rebekahs, and for the sake of their own children they violate the most sacred duties, forgetting the common kinship that binds the whole family on earth together. Yet reason seems to say that those who let one duty or affection swallow up all the rest lack the heart or mind to fulfil even that one conscientiously. It then loses the venerable appearance of a duty and takes on the fantastic shape of a whim.

Since the care of children in infancy is one of the great duties that nature has attached to the female character, this duty, properly considered, would supply many strong arguments for strengthening the female understanding.

The formation of the mind must begin very early, and the temper in particular needs the most judicious attention — an attention that women cannot give who love their children only because they are their children, and who look no further for the foundation of their duty than the feelings of the moment. It is this lack of reason in their affections that so often makes women run to extremes, and be either the most doting or the most careless and unnatural of mothers.

To be a good mother, a woman must have good sense, and that independence of mind which few women possess who are taught to depend entirely on their husbands. Meek wives are, in general, foolish mothers: they want their children to love them best and to side with them secretly against the father, who is held up as a bogeyman. If the children are to be punished, even though they have offended the mother, the father must inflict the punishment; he must be the judge in all disputes. But I shall discuss this subject more fully when I treat private education; for now I only mean to insist that unless woman’s understanding is enlarged, and her character made firmer by being allowed to govern her own conduct, she will never have enough sense or command of temper to manage her children properly. Indeed, her parental affection hardly deserves the name if it does not lead her to nurse her children at the breast, because carrying out this duty is equally suited to inspire maternal and filial affection; and it is the indispensable duty of men and women to fulfil the duties that give rise to affections, since these are the surest safeguards against vice. Natural affection, as it is called, I believe to be a very weak tie; affections must grow out of the habitual exercise of mutual sympathy; and what sympathy does a mother exercise who sends her baby to a nurse, and takes it back from the nurse only to send it to school?

In the exercise of their natural feelings, providence has given women a natural substitute for love for the time when the lover becomes only a friend and mutual confidence replaces overstrained admiration: a child then gently twists tight again the slackening cord, and shared care produces a new mutual sympathy. But a child, though a pledge of affection, will not enliven it if both father and mother are content to hand the charge over to hirelings; for those who do their duty by proxy should not complain if they miss the reward of duty — parental affection produces filial duty.
